reminder: A monomial is a product of [variables](c:variable), each raised to a [natural number](c:natural-number) power.
definition: A monomial in the [variables](c:variable) $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a product $x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ with every exponent $a_i$ a [natural number](c:natural-number). Each summand of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) is a monomial, and some authors keep the coefficient and call $c\,x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ a monomial.
examples: $x^2y$, $x$ and $1$ are monomials in $x,y$ (the exponents are $2,1$; $1,0$; $0,0$).
In Dickson's lemma, the monomial $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ is the same data as the vector $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.
Non-example: $x+y$ is a sum of two monomials, so it is not one monomial; $x^{-1}$ and $\sqrt{x}$ are not monomials, because the exponents are not natural numbers.

steps: Take a monomial $m=x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
Read $m$ as the sum with one summand, the term $1\cdot m$.
That sum is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with a single nonzero coefficient.
So every monomial is a polynomial, and every polynomial is a finite sum of monomials with coefficients.
links.why: It shows that a polynomial is built from monomials, and that a monomial is the one-term case.

reminder: A monotone operator $T$ satisfies $\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle\ge0$ for all $x$ and $y$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$. A map $T:X\to X^*$ is monotone when $\langle Tx-Ty,\,x-y\rangle\ge0$ for all $x,y\in X$, where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the pairing of $X^*$ with $X$. In a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) this pairing is the inner product.
examples: On $X=\mathbb{R}$, a map $T$ is monotone exactly when it is nondecreasing.
The identity map on a Hilbert space is monotone, because $\langle x-y,x-y\rangle=\|x-y\|^2\ge0$.
The gradient of a differentiable [convex function](c:convex-function) on a Hilbert space is monotone (Kachurovskii's theorem).
Non-example: $T(x)=-x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not monotone, because $(Tx-Ty)(x-y)=-(x-y)^2<0$ for $x\ne y$.

steps: Take a nondecreasing function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, and treat $\mathbb{R}$ as its own dual space.
For $x\ge y$ we have $f(x)\ge f(y)$, so $(f(x)-f(y))(x-y)\ge0$.
For $x<y$ both factors are not positive, so the product is again not negative.
So $f$ is a monotone operator, and every monotone operator on $\mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing.
links.why: It shows that monotone operators carry the idea of an increasing function to Banach spaces.

reminder: A Morse function is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) whose [critical points](c:critical-point) are all [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-critical-point).
definition: A Morse function on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ such that, at every [critical point](c:critical-point) $p$ (where $df_p=0$), the [Hessian](c:hessian) of $f$ in a chart is an invertible matrix. A critical point with this property is called [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-critical-point).
examples: $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has the single critical point $0$ with Hessian $(2)$, so it is a Morse function.
The height function on a torus that stands upright has four critical points (a minimum, two saddles and a maximum), and all are nondegenerate.
Non-example: $f(x)=x^3$ has the critical point $0$ with Hessian $(0)$, so it is not a Morse function.

steps: Take a Morse function $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ on a smooth manifold $M$.
By definition $f$ is smooth, so it is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function).
The Morse case adds one condition: the Hessian is invertible at every critical point.
links.why: It shows what the Morse condition adds to smoothness: invertible Hessians at all critical points.

reminder: A natural transformation between [functors](c:functor) $F,G$ is a family $\eta_X:FX\to GX$ that commutes with every morphism.
definition: Let $F,G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ be [functors](c:functor) between [categories](c:category). A natural transformation $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$ gives, for each object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$, a morphism $\eta_X:F(X)\to G(X)$ of $\mathcal{D}$ such that $G(f)\circ\eta_X=\eta_Y\circ F(f)$ for every morphism $f:X\to Y$ of $\mathcal{C}$. This says that a [commutative diagram](c:commutative-diagram), the naturality square, commutes for every $f$.
examples: The evaluation maps $V\to V^{**}$ form a natural transformation from the identity functor to the double dual functor on vector spaces.
The maps that reverse a list, one for each set $X$, form a natural transformation from the list functor to itself.

Non-example: on finite-dimensional vector spaces, let $\eta_V$ be the identity if $\dim V$ is even and the zero map if $\dim V$ is odd. The square fails for the inclusion $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$, so $\eta$ is not natural.

steps: Take a natural isomorphism $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$, so each component $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism.
In particular each $\eta_X$ is a morphism, and the naturality squares commute.
So $\eta$ is a natural transformation.
A natural transformation is a natural isomorphism exactly when every component $\eta_X$ is invertible.
links.why: It shows that a natural isomorphism is a natural transformation whose components are all isomorphisms.

reminder: A neighborhood of a point $x$ is a set that contains an [open set](c:open-set) that contains $x$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $x\in X$. A subset $N\subseteq X$ is a neighborhood of $x$ when there is an [open set](c:open-set) $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq N$. A neighborhood need not be open; some authors call only open sets neighborhoods.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the closed interval $[x-1,x+1]$ is a neighborhood of $x$, because it contains the open interval $(x-1,x+1)$.
Every open set $U$ with $x\in U$ is a neighborhood of $x$.
Non-example: $[0,1]$ is not a neighborhood of $1$ in $\mathbb{R}$, because every open set that contains $1$ also contains numbers greater than $1$.

steps: Take an open set $U$ with $x\in U$.
The set $U$ contains the open set $U$, and that open set contains $x$.
So $U$ is a neighborhood of $x$.
An open neighbourhood is a neighborhood that is also an open set.
links.why: It shows that every neighborhood contains an open one, so open neighbourhoods carry all the information.

reminder: Newton's method improves a guess $x_n$ for a [root](c:root) of $f$ to $x_n-f(x_n)/f'(x_n)$.
definition: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function with a [derivative](c:derivative) $f'$, and choose a start value $x_0$. Newton's method defines [recursively](c:recursion) $x_{n+1}=x_n-f(x_n)/f'(x_n)$ while $f'(x_n)\ne0$; here $x_{n+1}$ is the point where the tangent line of $f$ at $x_n$ meets the $x$-axis. The aim is that the sequence $x_n$ shows [convergence](c:convergence) to a [root](c:root) of $f$ in the [real numbers](c:real-number).
examples: For $f(x)=x^2-2$ and $x_0=1$ the iterates are $1$, $3/2$, $17/12$, $577/408$, which approach $\sqrt2$.
Near a simple root, the error shrinks about quadratically at each step.
The method can fail: for $f(x)=x^{1/3}$ the step is $x_{n+1}=-2x_n$, so the iterates move away from the root $0$.
Non-example: bisection also finds roots of continuous functions, but it halves an interval and uses no derivative, so it is not Newton's method.

reminder: A nondeterministic [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) may have several possible moves at each step, and it accepts when some run accepts.
definition: A nondeterministic [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) is a Turing machine whose transition relation may allow zero, one or several moves from each [configuration](c:cfg), instead of exactly one. It accepts an input when at least one sequence of moves from the start configuration reaches an accepting state.
examples: A machine for the set of composite numbers guesses a number $d$ with $1<d<n$ and checks that $d$ divides $n$; it accepts $n$ exactly when some guess works.
A machine for satisfiability guesses a truth assignment and checks every clause in polynomial time, which places the problem in [NP](c:np-complexity-class).
Non-example: a probabilistic Turing machine that tosses coins is not nondeterministic, because it accepts by the probability of acceptance and not by the existence of one accepting run.

steps: Take a deterministic Turing machine with transition function $\delta$.
View $\delta$ as a relation that gives exactly one move from each configuration.
Then the machine is a nondeterministic Turing machine with only one run on each input.
That single run accepts exactly when the deterministic machine accepts.
links.why: It shows that every deterministic machine is a nondeterministic one with a single run on each input.

reminder: Normal ordering moves every creation operator to the left of every annihilation operator in a product.
definition: For a product of [creation and annihilation operators](c:creation-and-annihilation-operators), the normal ordering $:A_1\cdots A_n:$ is the product rearranged so that all creation operators stand to the left of all annihilation operators, as if the operators commuted (bosons) or anticommuted (fermions, with a sign change for each swap). It is extended linearly to sums of such products.
examples: For one boson mode, $:aa^\dagger:=a^\dagger a$, while the plain product is $aa^\dagger=a^\dagger a+1$.
For one fermion mode, $:cc^\dagger:=-c^\dagger c$, because one swap gives one sign.
Non-example: the plain product $aa^\dagger$ is not normal ordered, because an annihilation operator stands left of a creation operator, and it differs from $:aa^\dagger:$ by the commutator $1$.

reminder: Two vectors are orthogonal when their [inner product](c:inner-product-space) is zero.
definition: In an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), vectors $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal, written $u\perp v$, when $\langle u,v\rangle=0$. Two sets of vectors, such as two subspaces, are orthogonal when every vector of one is orthogonal to every vector of the other; two functions are orthogonal when $\int_a^b f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx=0$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product, $(1,2)$ and $(2,-1)$ are orthogonal, because $1\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)=0$.
The functions $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are orthogonal in $L^2([-\pi,\pi])$, because $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin x\cos x\,dx=0$.
Non-example: $(1,1)$ and $(1,2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have dot product $3\ne0$, so they are not orthogonal.

steps: Take two lines through a point of the plane, with direction vectors $u$ and $v$.
The lines are perpendicular when the angle $\theta$ between them is $90^\circ$.
Since $\cos\theta=\langle u,v\rangle/(\|u\|\|v\|)$, this holds exactly when $\langle u,v\rangle=0$.
So perpendicular lines have orthogonal direction vectors, and orthogonality extends this to every inner product space.
links.why: It shows that orthogonality is the algebraic form of the right angle, and that it works in any inner product space.

reminder: The $p$-adic valuation $v_p(n)$ counts how many times the [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ divides $n$.
definition: For a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ and a nonzero [integer](c:integer) $n$, $v_p(n)$ is the largest $k\ge0$ such that $p^k$ divides $n$ (see [divisibility](c:divisibility)), and $v_p(0)=\infty$. For a nonzero [rational number](c:rational-number) $a/b$ it is $v_p(a/b)=v_p(a)-v_p(b)$.
examples: Non-example: $\Omega(12)=3$ counts all prime factors with multiplicity, but $v_2(12)=2$ counts only the prime $2$.

steps: Define $v=v_p$ on the rational numbers; it satisfies $v(xy)=v(x)+v(y)$.
It also satisfies $v(x+y)\ge\min(v(x),v(y))$.
Its values are integers (and $\infty$ at $0$), and $v(p)=1$ shows that it takes every integer value.
So $v_p$ is a [discrete valuation](c:discrete-valuation) of the field $\mathbb{Q}$.
links.why: It shows that $v_p$ has every property of a discrete valuation, so the general results apply to it.

reminder: A $p$-group is a [group](c:group) in which every element has order a power of the prime $p$.
definition: Let $p$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number). A [group](c:group) $G$ is a $p$-group when the [order](c:order-of-an-element) of every element is a power of $p$. A [finite group](c:finite-group) is a $p$-group exactly when its order is $p^n$ for some $n\ge0$.
examples: $\mathbb{Z}/9\mathbb{Z}$ is a $3$-group, and the dihedral group of order $8$ is a $2$-group.
The Prüfer group $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}$ is an infinite $p$-group, because each of its elements has order a power of $p$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ is not a $p$-group for any prime $p$, because it has elements of order $2$ and of order $3$.

steps: Take a $p$-group $G$ and an element $g\in G$.
The order of $g$ is a power $p^k$, so it is finite.
A group in which every element has finite order is a [torsion group](c:torsion-group).
The $p$-group case adds that every order is a power of the one prime $p$.
links.why: It shows that a $p$-group is a torsion group in which only one prime occurs in the orders.

reminder: Functions $f_n$ converge pointwise to $f$ when $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at every single point $x$.
definition: A sequence of [functions](c:function) $f_n:X\to\mathbb{R}$ converges pointwise to $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ when, for every $x\in X$, the [limit of the sequence](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of numbers $f_n(x)$ is $f(x)$. In epsilon form: for every $x$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$, which may depend on $x$, such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$. The same definition works for values in any [metric space](c:metric-space).
examples: $f_n(x)=x/n$ converges pointwise to $0$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
$f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$ converges pointwise to $0$ for $x<1$ and to $1$ at $x=1$, so the limit function is not continuous.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)$ does not converge pointwise on $\mathbb{R}$; at $x=\pi/2$ the values are $1,0,-1,0,\dots$ and have no limit.

steps: Let $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $X$.
Fix $\varepsilon>0$; one index $N$ gives $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for all $x$ and all $n\ge N$.
In particular, for each fixed $x$ this inequality holds for all $n\ge N$.
So $f_n$ converges pointwise to $f$; the converse fails when $N$ must depend on $x$.
links.why: It shows that uniform convergence is pointwise convergence with one index $N$ for all points.

reminder: A Poisson variable with mean $\lambda$ takes the value $k$ with probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.
definition: For a real number $\lambda>0$, the Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$ is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ with $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ for each $k$; it uses the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) and the [factorial](c:factorial). Its mean and its variance are both $\lambda$.
examples: The number of calls that reach a call centre in one hour is often modelled as Poisson, with $\lambda$ equal to the average number of calls.
For $\lambda=2$ we get $P(X=0)=e^{-2}\approx0.135$ and $P(X=1)=2e^{-2}\approx0.271$.
The [binomial distribution](c:binomial-distribution) with $n$ trials and success probability $\lambda/n$ approaches the Poisson distribution as $n\to\infty$.
Non-example: the binomial distribution with $n=10$ and $p=1/2$ is not Poisson, because it takes only the values $0,\dots,10$.

steps: Take $\lambda>0$ and set $p_k=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ for $k=0,1,2,\dots$.
Each $p_k$ is positive, and $\sum_kp_k=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1$.
So the numbers $p_k$ form a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the natural numbers.
The Poisson case is the one whose weights have exactly this formula.
links.why: It shows that the Poisson formula gives a true probability distribution, because the weights add up to $1$.

reminder: A real [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix) $A$ is positive definite when $x^TAx>0$ for every nonzero vector $x$.
definition: A real [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix) $A$ of size $n\times n$ is positive definite when $x^TAx>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Equivalently, all [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $A$ are positive. In the complex case, $A$ is Hermitian and $x^*Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$.
examples: The identity matrix $I$ is positive definite, because $x^TIx=\|x\|^2>0$ for $x\ne0$.
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $3$, so it is positive definite.
For every matrix $B$ with independent columns, $B^TB$ is positive definite.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $-1$, and $x^TAx=-2<0$ at $x=(1,-1)$, so it is not positive definite.

steps: Take a positive-definite matrix $A$, so $x^TAx>0$ for all $x\ne0$.
Then $x^TAx\ge0$ for all $x\ne0$, and $x^TAx=0$ at $x=0$.
So $A$ is a [positive semidefinite matrix](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix).
The definite case adds that $x^TAx=0$ only for $x=0$.
links.why: It shows that positive definite means positive semidefinite with no nonzero null direction.

reminder: A predictable [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) has a value at each time $t$ that the information strictly before $t$ determines.
definition: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ be a [filtered probability space](c:filtered-probability-space) with [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_t)$. The predictable [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) on $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is generated by the sets $\{0\}\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_0$ and $(s,t]\times A$ with $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$. A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $H$ is predictable when $(t,\omega)\mapsto H_t(\omega)$ is measurable for this sigma-algebra.
examples: Every left-continuous adapted process is predictable, such as the left limit $N_{t-}$ of a Poisson process $N$.
The simple integrand $H=\mathbf 1_{(s,u]\times A}$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ is predictable: it bets at time $s$ using only the information up to $s$.
Non-example: a Poisson process $N_t$ is adapted and right-continuous but not predictable, because a jump at time $t$ cannot be foreseen from the information before $t$.

steps: Take a predictable process $H$ and a time $t$.
For a generating set $(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$, the section at time $t$ is $A$ or empty, so it lies in $\mathcal F_t$.
The sets whose section at time $t$ lies in $\mathcal F_t$ form a sigma-algebra, so they include all predictable sets.
So $H_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and $H$ is an adapted [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process).
links.why: It shows that predictable processes are adapted, with the extra condition that they use only strictly earlier information.

reminder: A preference relation says which of two alternatives is at least as good, and it is complete and transitive.
definition: A preference relation on a [set](c:set) $X$ of alternatives is a binary [relation](c:relation) $\succsim$ on $X$ that is complete (for all $x,y$, either $x\succsim y$ or $y\succsim x$) and transitive (if $x\succsim y$ and $y\succsim z$, then $x\succsim z$). Write $x\succ y$ for strict preference, when $x\succsim y$ but not $y\succsim x$, and $x\sim y$ for indifference, when both hold.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, let $x\succsim y$ mean $x\ge y$; indifference is then equality.
A person ranks pizza above pasta, is indifferent between pasta and salad, and ranks both above soup.
Non-example: the cyclic ranking $a\succ b$, $b\succ c$, $c\succ a$ is not a preference relation, because it is not transitive.

steps: Take a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$.
Completeness with $y=x$ gives $x\succsim x$ for every $x$, so $\succsim$ is reflexive.
The relation is transitive by definition, so $\succsim$ is a [preorder](c:is-preorder).
The preference case adds completeness: any two elements are comparable.
links.why: It shows that a preference relation is a preorder in which every two alternatives can be compared.

steps: Take a [total order](c:total-order) $\le$ on a set $X$.
It is reflexive, transitive and complete, so it is a preference relation.
Here $x\sim y$ holds only when $x=y$, because $\le$ is antisymmetric.
So a total order is a preference relation with no indifference between different alternatives.
links.why: It shows that a total order is the case of strict ranking, and that indifference is what the general case adds.

reminder: A prime power is a number $p^n$ where $p$ is a [prime](c:prime-number) and $n\ge1$.
definition: A prime power is a natural number of the form $p^n$, where $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number) and $n\ge1$ is a [natural number](c:natural-number). Equivalently, it is a number greater than $1$ with exactly one prime divisor.
examples: Every prime number $p$ is a prime power, with $n=1$.
Non-example: $12=2^2\cdot3$ has two different prime divisors, so it is not a prime power; $1$ is not one either, because $n\ge1$.

steps: Take a prime number $p$.
Write $p=p^1$, so the exponent $n=1$ is allowed.
So $p$ is a prime power.
A prime power may have $n>1$, as in $9=3^2$, so the two concepts differ.
links.why: It shows that prime powers are the primes together with their higher powers.

reminder: A primitive polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$ has coefficients whose [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) is $1$.
definition: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) over a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain) $R$, such as $\mathbb{Z}$, is primitive when the [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of its coefficients is a unit of $R$. Equivalently, no prime element of $R$ divides all coefficients.
examples: $2x^2+3x+4$ is primitive over $\mathbb{Z}$, because $\gcd(2,3,4)=1$.
Every monic polynomial is primitive, such as $x^2-2$, because one coefficient is $1$.
Non-example: $2x^2+4x+6=2(x^2+2x+3)$ is not primitive, because $2$ divides every coefficient.

steps: Take a polynomial $f$ of positive degree that is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Suppose a prime $q$ divides every coefficient, so $f=q\,g$ with $\deg g>0$.
Then $q$ and $g$ are not units, and their product is $f$, which contradicts irreducibility.
So no prime divides all coefficients, and $f$ is primitive.
links.why: It shows that primitivity is a necessary condition for a nonconstant integer polynomial to be irreducible.

reminder: Probability gives each event a number in $[0,1]$, the whole space gets $1$, and disjoint events add.
definition: A probability is a function $P$ that assigns to each event $A$ of a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal F$ on a set $\Omega$ a number $P(A)\in[0,1]$, with $P(\Omega)=1$ and $P(\bigcup_iA_i)=\sum_iP(A_i)$ for every countable family of disjoint events $A_i$. In other words, $P$ is a [measure](c:measure) of total mass $1$.
examples: For a fair die, $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}$ and $P(A)=|A|/6$, so $P(\text{even})=1/2$.
On $[0,1]$ with the uniform distribution, $P([a,b])=b-a$ for $0\le a\le b\le1$.
Non-example: $\mu(A)=2|A|/6$ on the same die is a measure but not a probability, because $\mu(\Omega)=2$.

steps: Take a probability $P$ on a sigma-algebra $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $\Omega$.
Additivity over countable disjoint unions gives $P(\varnothing)=0$, because $P(\Omega)$ is finite.
So $P$ is a [measure](c:measure) on the [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$.
The probability case adds the normalization $P(\Omega)=1$.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about measures also holds for probabilities, and that normalization is the only addition.

reminder: A pseudoholomorphic curve is a smooth map $u$ from a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) to an almost complex manifold with $du\circ j=J\circ du$.
definition: Let $(\Sigma,j)$ be a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) and $(M,\omega)$ a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) with a compatible [almost complex structure](c:almost-complex-structure) $J$. A [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $u:\Sigma\to M$ is pseudoholomorphic (or $J$-holomorphic) when its [differential](c:differential) satisfies $du\circ j=J\circ du$, so that $du$ is complex linear at every point.
examples: A holomorphic map from a Riemann surface to $\mathbb{C}^n$ with its standard $J$ is pseudoholomorphic.
A line $\mathbb{CP}^1\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ with the standard complex structure is a pseudoholomorphic curve.
Non-example: $u(z)=\bar z$ from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ is not pseudoholomorphic for the standard $J$, because $du\circ j=-J\circ du$ (the map is antilinear).

steps: Take $\Sigma=\mathbb{C}$ with $j=i$ and $M=\mathbb{C}$ with $J=i$.
Then $du\circ j=J\circ du$ says $du(iv)=i\,du(v)$ for all tangent vectors $v$.
This complex linearity of the real differential is the [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations).
So $u$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function); a general $J$ replaces the number $i$ in the target.
links.why: It shows that pseudoholomorphic curves are the Cauchy-Riemann equation in a target without complex coordinates.

reminder: A quantum state is a positive operator of trace $1$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space); a unit vector gives a pure state.
definition: A quantum state of a system with [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\mathcal H$ is a [density operator](c:density-operator) $\rho$ on $\mathcal H$: a [positive operator](c:positive-operator) that is a [trace-class operator](c:trace-class-operator) with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. It is a [pure state](c:pure-state) when $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ for a unit vector $\psi$, and mixed otherwise.
examples: A qubit in the vector $\psi=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$ is in a pure state.
The maximally mixed state $\rho=I/2$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$ has trace $1$ and rank $2$, so it is a mixed state.
Non-example: $\rho=I$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$ is positive but has trace $2$, so it is not a state.

steps: Take a pure state, given by a unit vector $\psi\in\mathcal H$.
Form $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$, which is positive with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$.
So $\rho$ is a density operator, hence a quantum state.
The pure case adds that $\rho$ has rank one, and vectors that differ by a phase give the same $\rho$.
links.why: It shows that pure states are the rank-one quantum states, and that mixed states are weighted averages of them.

steps: Take a density operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H$ and the star-algebra $B(\mathcal H)$ of bounded operators.
Define $\omega(A)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for every bounded operator $A$.
This $\omega$ is linear, positive because $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$, and normalized by $\omega(1)=1$.
So $\omega$ is a [state on a star-algebra](c:state-on-a-star-algebra).
links.why: It shows that Hilbert-space states are the special case of algebraic states on the algebra of bounded operators.

reminder: A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is quasi-compact when the preimage of every quasi-compact open set of $Y$ is quasi-compact.
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is quasi-compact when $f^{-1}(U)$ is a quasi-compact space (see [compact space](c:compact-space)) for every quasi-compact [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq Y$. It is enough to check this for every [affine](c:affine-scheme) open subset $U$ of $Y$.
examples: Every morphism of affine schemes is quasi-compact, because the preimage of a basic open set $D(a)$ is the affine open set $D(\varphi(a))$.
Every affine morphism, such as a closed immersion, is quasi-compact, because the preimage of an affine open set is affine.

Non-example: for $A=k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$, the open immersion of $\bigcup_iD(x_i)$ into $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is not quasi-compact, because the preimage of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is $\bigcup_iD(x_i)$ and no finite subfamily covers it.

steps: Take a quasi-compact space $X$ and the map $f:X\to\{*\}$ to a point.
The quasi-compact open sets of the point are $\varnothing$ and $\{*\}$, with preimages $\varnothing$ and $X$.
Both preimages are quasi-compact, so $f$ is a quasi-compact map.
Conversely, if $f:X\to\{*\}$ is quasi-compact, then $X=f^{-1}(\{*\})$ is quasi-compact.
links.why: It shows that a space is quasi-compact exactly when its map to a point is, so the relative notion extends the absolute one.

reminder: A quasi-isomorphism is a [chain map](c:chain-map) that induces an isomorphism on homology in every degree.
definition: A [chain map](c:chain-map) $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ between [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) is a quasi-isomorphism when the induced map $H_n(f):H_n(C_\bullet)\to H_n(D_\bullet)$ on [homology](c:homology) is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) for every $n$. In the [derived category](c:derived-category), quasi-isomorphisms become isomorphisms.
examples: A projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ of an abelian group $A$ is a quasi-isomorphism from $P_\bullet$ to $A$ placed in degree $0$.
The zero map $0\to C_\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism exactly when $C_\bullet$ is exact.
Non-example: multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, viewed as a chain map of complexes in degree $0$, induces multiplication by $2$ on $H_0=\mathbb{Z}$, which is not an isomorphism.

steps: Take a chain homotopy equivalence $f$ with a chain map $g$ such that $gf$ and $fg$ are chain homotopic to the identities.
Chain homotopic maps induce the same map on homology, so $H_n(g)H_n(f)=\mathrm{id}$ and $H_n(f)H_n(g)=\mathrm{id}$.
So each $H_n(f)$ is an isomorphism, and $f$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
The converse needs extra conditions, such as bounded-below complexes of projective modules.
links.why: It shows that every homotopy equivalence is a quasi-isomorphism, and that the converse is false in general.

reminder: The radical of an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ is the set of elements that have a power in $I$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$. The radical $\sqrt I$ is the set $\{r\in R:r^n\in I\text{ for some }n\ge1\}$, which is again an ideal that contains $I$.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, $\sqrt{(12)}=(6)$, because $r^n$ is divisible by $12=2^2\cdot3$ exactly when $2$ and $3$ divide $r$.
Non-example: $5$ is not in $\sqrt{(12)}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, because no power of $5$ is divisible by $12$.

steps: Take the zero ideal $I=(0)$ of the commutative ring $R$.
Then $\sqrt{(0)}=\{r\in R:r^n=0\text{ for some }n\ge1\}$.
This is the set of nilpotent elements, the [nilradical](c:nilradical) of $R$.
So the nilradical is the radical of the zero ideal, and $\sqrt I$ is the preimage of the nilradical of $R/I$.
links.why: It shows that the radical of an ideal measures nilpotence modulo that ideal.

reminder: A rectangle is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) with four right angles.
definition: A rectangle is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) in the plane whose four [angles](c:angle) are all right angles ($90^\circ$). Its opposite sides are equal and parallel, and its two diagonals have equal length.
examples: A sheet of A4 paper is a rectangle.
Every square is a rectangle.
Non-example: a rhombus with angles $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ has four equal sides but no right angle, so it is not a rectangle.

steps: Take a rectangle $ABCD$ with all four angles equal to $90^\circ$.
The sides $AB$ and $CD$ are both perpendicular to $BC$, so they are parallel.
The same argument shows that $BC$ and $AD$ are parallel.
So $ABCD$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) whose angles are right angles.
links.why: It shows that a rectangle is a parallelogram with one right angle, and that its other properties follow.

steps: Take a [square](c:square), a quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles.
It has four right angles, so it is a rectangle.
A rectangle is a square exactly when two adjacent sides are equal.
links.why: It shows that a square is a rectangle with equal adjacent sides.

reminder: A recurrence relation defines each term of a [sequence](c:sequence) from the terms before it.
definition: A recurrence relation of order $k$ is an equation $a_n=F(n,a_{n-1},\dots,a_{n-k})$ that defines each term of a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ from the $k$ terms before it, for all [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $n\ge k$. Together with the first $k$ terms, it determines the whole sequence.
examples: The Fibonacci numbers satisfy $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ with $F_0=0$ and $F_1=1$.
The running time of merge sort satisfies $T(n)=2T(n/2)+cn$, which relates a value to a value at a smaller argument.
Non-example: $a_n=n^2$ is a closed formula and not a recurrence, because it gives $a_n$ without any earlier term.

steps: Take a [linear recurrence](c:linear-recurrence) $a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+\dots+c_ka_{n-k}$ with constants $c_i$.
Its right side is a function $F(n,a_{n-1},\dots,a_{n-k})$ of the earlier terms.
So it is a recurrence relation of order $k$.
The linear case adds that $F$ is linear in $a_{n-1},\dots,a_{n-k}$.
links.why: It shows that a linear recurrence is a recurrence relation whose right side is linear in the earlier terms.

reminder: The resolvent of an operator $T$ at $\lambda$ is the inverse $(\lambda-T)^{-1}$, a bounded operator when $\lambda$ is outside the spectrum.
definition: Let $T$ be a [closed operator](c:closed-operator) on a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$. If a complex number $\lambda$ is not in the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) of $T$, then $\lambda-T$ has a bounded [inverse](c:inverse), and the resolvent is $R(\lambda,T)=(\lambda-T)^{-1}$, a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator). Some authors use $(T-\lambda)^{-1}$ instead.
examples: For a square matrix $A$, $R(\lambda,A)=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}$ exists for every $\lambda$ that is not an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue).
For multiplication by a bounded function $m$ on $L^2$, the resolvent is multiplication by $1/(\lambda-m)$ when $\lambda$ lies outside the essential range of $m$.
In the Hille-Yosida theorem, the generator $A$ of a contraction semigroup has $\|R(\lambda,A)\|\le1/\lambda$ for every $\lambda>0$.
Non-example: at an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ the operator $\lambda-T$ has a nonzero kernel, so it has no inverse and there is no resolvent at $\lambda$.

reminder: The Riemann integral of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is the limit of [Riemann sums](c:riemann-sum) as the partitions get finer.
definition: A function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable with integral $I$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $|S-I|<\varepsilon$ for every [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) of the [interval](c:interval) $[a,b]$ with mesh less than $\delta$, where $S$ is the [Riemann sum](c:riemann-sum) of $f$ for that partition. The number $I$ is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) of these sums and is written $\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$.
examples: Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, for example $\int_0^1x^2\,dx=1/3$.
Every monotone function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable.

Non-example: the Dirichlet function, equal to $1$ on the rationals and $0$ on the irrationals, is not Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, because Riemann sums with rational tags give $1$ and those with irrational tags give $0$.

steps: Take a Riemann integrable function $f$ on $[a,b]$ with integral $I$.
Choose nested partitions whose lower and upper step functions $l_k\le f\le u_k$ have integrals that both tend to $I$.
Then $\lim l_k=\lim u_k=f$ almost everywhere, so $f$ is Lebesgue measurable.
So $f$ is Lebesgue integrable, and its [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) equals $I$.
links.why: It shows that the Riemann integral agrees with the Lebesgue integral on every function where it is defined.

steps: Let a gauge be a function $\delta:[a,b]\to(0,\infty)$, and call a tagged partition $\delta$-fine when each cell lies in $(t_i-\delta(t_i),t_i+\delta(t_i))$ around its tag $t_i$.
The Henstock integral asks, for each $\varepsilon>0$, for some gauge $\delta$ with $|S-I|<\varepsilon$ on all $\delta$-fine tagged partitions.
Take the constant gauge $\delta(t)=\delta_0/2$; every $\delta$-fine tagged partition has mesh less than $\delta_0$.
So a Riemann integrable function is Henstock integrable with the same integral, and the gauge may now vary from point to point.
links.why: It shows that the Henstock integral is the Riemann integral with a gauge that may change from point to point.

reminder: A ruler-and-compass construction finds new points as intersections of lines and circles drawn from known points.
definition: Start with a finite set of known [points](c:point) in the plane. A step of the construction draws a [line](c:line) through two known points, or a [circle](c:circle) with a known centre that passes through another known point, and every intersection point of two such lines or circles becomes a known point. A point is constructible when it becomes known after finitely many steps.
examples: To bisect a segment, draw a circle about each end point through the other end point; the line through the two intersection points is the perpendicular bisector.
To build an equilateral triangle on a segment $AB$, draw the circles about $A$ and about $B$ with radius $AB$; an intersection point is the third vertex.
Non-example: a marked ruler (neusis) can trisect an angle, but that is not a ruler-and-compass construction, because the marks on the ruler are not allowed.

reminder: A Schwartz function is [smooth](c:smooth-function), and it and all its derivatives decay faster than any power of $\|x\|$.
definition: A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) is a Schwartz function when it is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) and $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f$ is bounded for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, where $\partial^\beta f$ is a [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) of $f$. Equivalently, for every $\beta$ and every $N$ there is $C$ with $|\partial^\beta f(x)|\le C(1+\|x\|)^{-N}$.
examples: The Gaussian $e^{-\|x\|^2}$ is a Schwartz function.
Every smooth function with [compact support](c:compact-support) is a Schwartz function.
Non-example: $1/(1+x^2)$ is smooth but not Schwartz, because it decays only like $x^{-2}$ and $x^3f(x)$ is unbounded.

steps: Take a Schwartz function $f$.
By definition $f$ is smooth, so it is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function).
The Schwartz case adds a bound on $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f$ for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$.
links.why: It shows that a Schwartz function is a smooth function with decay of all derivatives.

steps: Take a smooth function $\varphi$ with compact support in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Each derivative $\partial^\beta\varphi$ is continuous with compact support, so it is bounded and zero outside a ball.
Then $x^\alpha\partial^\beta\varphi$ is bounded for all $\alpha,\beta$.
So $\varphi$ is a Schwartz function.
links.why: It shows that compactly supported smooth functions are Schwartz functions, so Schwartz results cover them.

reminder: The second fundamental form of a surface measures how the surface bends away from its tangent plane.
definition: Let $S\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be a [regular surface](c:regular-surface) with a unit [normal vector](c:normal-vector) field $N$. At each point $p$ the second fundamental form is the [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $\mathrm{II}_p(v,w)=-\langle dN_p(v),w\rangle$ on the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pS$. For a submanifold of a Riemannian manifold the same idea gives $\mathrm{II}(X,Y)=(\nabla_XY)^\perp$, the normal part of the [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection) applied to tangent fields.
examples: For a plane, $N$ is constant, so $dN=0$ and $\mathrm{II}=0$.
For the unit sphere with outward normal $N(p)=p$, we get $dN=\mathrm{id}$ and $\mathrm{II}_p(v,w)=-\langle v,w\rangle$.

Non-example: the [first fundamental form](c:first-fundamental-form) $\langle v,w\rangle$ measures lengths along the surface and does not see bending; a cylinder and a plane have the same first form locally but different second forms.

reminder: An endomorphism is semisimple when every [invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace) has an invariant complement.
definition: Let $V$ be a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) over a field $k$. An [endomorphism](c:endomorphism) $T:V\to V$ is semisimple when every $T$-[invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace) $W$ has a $T$-invariant complement $W'$ with $V=W\oplus W'$. Equivalently, the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $T$ is a product of distinct irreducible polynomials over $k$; over an algebraically closed field this means that $T$ is [diagonalizable](c:diagonalizable-matrix).
examples: A diagonalizable matrix, such as $\mathrm{diag}(1,2)$, is semisimple.
The rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by $90^\circ$ is semisimple over $\mathbb{R}$, because its minimal polynomial $x^2+1$ is irreducible; it is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has the invariant line spanned by $e_1$ but no invariant complement, and its minimal polynomial is $(x-1)^2$.

steps: Take a diagonalizable endomorphism $T$ with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$.
Its minimal polynomial is $(x-\lambda_1)\cdots(x-\lambda_r)$, a product of distinct linear factors.
Linear polynomials are irreducible, so $T$ is semisimple.
The converse holds over an algebraically closed field but fails over $\mathbb{R}$, as the rotation by $90^\circ$ shows.
links.why: It shows that semisimple is diagonalizable without the need for the eigenvalues to lie in the field.

steps: Make $V$ a module over the polynomial ring $k[x]$ by letting $x$ act as $T$.
The $k[x]$-submodules of $V$ are exactly the $T$-invariant subspaces.
So $T$ is semisimple exactly when every submodule has a complement, that is, when $V$ is a [semisimple module](c:is-semisimple-module).
links.why: It shows that semisimple endomorphisms are the semisimple modules over $k[x]$, so module theory applies.

reminder: A separating [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) has one of two sets on each of its two closed sides.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the [inner product](c:inner-product-space) $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. A [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $H=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=b\}$ with $a\ne0$ separates $A$ and $B$ when $\langle a,x\rangle\le b$ for all $x\in A$ and $\langle a,x\rangle\ge b$ for all $x\in B$. It separates them strictly when both inequalities are strict.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, the line $x=3/2$ separates the unit disk from the disk of radius $1$ centred at $(3,0)$, and it does so strictly.
For two disjoint nonempty [convex sets](c:convex-set) in $\mathbb{R}^n$, a separating hyperplane always exists.
Non-example: no line separates the unit disk from the circle of radius $2$ around it, because the circle lies on both sides of every line that has the disk on one side.

steps: Take a separating hyperplane $H=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=b\}$ for sets $A$ and $B$.
It is a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane), the level set of the linear functional $x\mapsto\langle a,x\rangle$.
The separating case adds that $A$ and $B$ lie in the two closed half-spaces of $H$.
links.why: It shows that separation is a condition on a hyperplane relative to two sets.

reminder: A small [category](c:category) has a [set](c:set) of objects and a set of morphisms, not a proper class.
definition: A [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is small when its collection of objects and its collection of morphisms are each a [small set](c:small-set), that is, a [set](c:set) of the chosen universe and not a proper class. A category that is not small, such as the category of all sets, is called a [large category](c:large-category).
examples: Every [monoid](c:monoid) is a small category with one object.
Every [partial order](c:partial-order) on a set is a small category, with one morphism $x\to y$ when $x\le y$.
Non-example: the category of all sets is not small, because its objects form a proper class.

steps: Take a small category $\mathcal C$.
It has objects, morphisms, composition and identities, as every [category](c:category) has.
The small case adds that the objects form a set and the morphisms form a set.
links.why: It shows that a small category is a category with a size condition, which lets us form sets and categories of categories.

steps: Take a [monoid](c:monoid) $(M,\cdot,1)$, a set with an associative product and a unit.
Let the category $BM$ have one object $*$ and let the morphisms $*\to*$ be the elements of $M$.
Composition is the product and the identity morphism is $1$.
The objects and the morphisms form sets, so $BM$ is a small category with exactly one object.
links.why: It shows that a monoid is a small category with one object.

reminder: A [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) is solvable when its [derived series](c:derived-series) reaches $0$ after finitely many steps.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra). Its [derived series](c:derived-series) is $\mathfrak g^{(0)}=\mathfrak g$ and $\mathfrak g^{(k+1)}=[\mathfrak g^{(k)},\mathfrak g^{(k)}]$, the span of all [brackets](c:lie-bracket) of pairs from $\mathfrak g^{(k)}$. The algebra $\mathfrak g$ is solvable when $\mathfrak g^{(k)}=0$ for some $k$.
examples: Every abelian Lie algebra is solvable, because $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]=0$ gives $\mathfrak g^{(1)}=0$.
The Lie algebra of upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices is solvable.
Non-example: $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ is not solvable, because $[\mathfrak{sl}_2,\mathfrak{sl}_2]=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so the derived series never gets smaller.

steps: Take a nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with lower central series $C^1=\mathfrak g$, $C^{k+1}=[\mathfrak g,C^k]$, and $C^m=0$.
By induction $\mathfrak g^{(k)}\subseteq C^{k+1}$, because $[\mathfrak g^{(k)},\mathfrak g^{(k)}]\subseteq[\mathfrak g,C^{k+1}]$.
So $\mathfrak g^{(m)}\subseteq C^{m+1}\subseteq C^m=0$.
Hence $\mathfrak g$ is solvable; the converse fails, because upper triangular matrices are solvable but not nilpotent.
links.why: It shows that every nilpotent Lie algebra is solvable, and that solvable is the weaker condition.

steps: Take a solvable Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.
It has a bracket, so it is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).
The solvable case adds that the derived series reaches $0$ after finitely many steps.
links.why: It shows that solvability is one condition on the derived series of a Lie algebra.

reminder: A straight line through two distinct [points](c:point) $P$ and $Q$ is the set of all $P+t(Q-P)$ with $t$ real.
definition: In the Euclidean [plane](c:plane), or in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), the straight line through two distinct [points](c:point) $P$ and $Q$ is the set $\{P+t(Q-P):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ with $t$ a [real number](c:real-number). It is the only straight line that contains both points, and the shortest path between two of its points is the piece of the line between them.
examples: In coordinates, the graph of $y=2x+1$ is a straight line.
The $x$-axis is the straight line through $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$.
Non-example: the graph of $y=x^2$ is not a straight line, because it contains $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ but not $(1/2,1/2)$.

steps: Take the Euclidean plane as a Riemannian manifold with the standard metric.
A [geodesic](c:geodesic) is a curve $\gamma$ with zero acceleration, $\gamma''=0$, in these coordinates.
The solutions are $\gamma(t)=P+tv$ with a constant vector $v$, which parametrize straight lines.
So the straight lines are exactly the geodesics of the plane.
links.why: It shows that geodesics extend the straight line to curved spaces.

steps: Take the straight line through $P$ and $Q$ in the plane, with direction $d=Q-P$.
Choose $a\ne0$ perpendicular to $d$, which is possible in two dimensions.
Then $\langle a,P+td\rangle=\langle a,P\rangle$ for every $t$, so the line lies in the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\langle a,P\rangle\}$.
Both sets have dimension one, so they are equal, and in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the lines are the hyperplanes.
links.why: It shows that the straight line in the plane is the first case of a hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

reminder: A first-order structure is a [set](c:set) with chosen constants, functions and relations that interpret the symbols of a language.
definition: Let $L$ be a first-order [signature](c:signature) of function symbols, relation symbols and constants. An $L$-structure $M$ is a nonempty [set](c:set) $|M|$, its universe, together with a [function](c:function) $f^M:|M|^n\to|M|$ for each $n$-ary function symbol $f$ (a constant is the case $n=0$) and a [relation](c:relation) $R^M\subseteq|M|^n$ for each $n$-ary relation symbol $R$.
examples: The integers with the operation $+$, the element $0$ and the relation $<$ form a structure for the language with these three symbols.
Every [group](c:group) is a structure for the language with symbols $\cdot$, $e$ and ${}^{-1}$.
Non-example: a set with a partial operation, such as division on $\mathbb{R}$ with $1/0$ undefined, does not interpret a binary function symbol, because the interpretation must be defined everywhere.

steps: Take the signature with a binary symbol $\cdot$, a constant $e$ and a unary symbol ${}^{-1}$.
Interpret the symbols in a [group](c:group) $G$ by its product, its identity and its inverse map.
Then $G$ is a structure for this signature.
The group axioms are sentences that this structure satisfies, so a group is a structure that is a [model](c:model) of them.
links.why: It shows that a group is a structure that satisfies the group axioms.

steps: Take the signature with one binary relation symbol $\le$.
Interpret $\le$ in a partially ordered set by its order relation.
Then the poset is a structure whose universe is its set of elements.
The axioms of reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity are sentences that this structure satisfies.
links.why: It shows that a partial order is a structure with one relation that satisfies three axioms.

reminder: A summable bound is a series of constants $M_n$ with $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $x$ and $\sum M_n<\infty$.
definition: Let $f_n:X\to\mathbb{C}$ be [functions](c:function) on a set $X$. A summable bound for $(f_n)$ is a sequence of numbers $M_n\ge0$ such that the [absolute value](c:absolute-value) satisfies $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $n$ and all $x\in X$, and the [series](c:series) $\sum_nM_n$ converges. Then $\sum_nf_n(x)$ shows [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence) at every $x$, as in the Weierstrass M-test.
examples: For $f_n(x)=x^n/n!$ on $|x|\le R$, the numbers $M_n=R^n/n!$ are a summable bound, because $\sum R^n/n!=e^R$.
For $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)/n^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the numbers $M_n=1/n^2$ are a summable bound.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1)$ has $\sup|f_n|=1$ for every $n$, so every bound has $M_n\ge1$ and $\sum M_n$ diverges.

steps: Take a series $\sum a_n$ of numbers that converges absolutely, so $\sum|a_n|<\infty$.
Let $X$ be a one-point set and set $f_n(x)=a_n$.
Then $M_n=|a_n|$ is a summable bound for $(f_n)$.
So absolute convergence is the case of a summable bound for functions on a single point.
links.why: It shows that a summable bound is absolute convergence that holds uniformly over a whole set of parameters.

reminder: The symmetric group $S_n$ consists of all [permutations](c:permutation) of $n$ objects, with composition as the product.
definition: For a [set](c:set) $X$, the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ is the [group](c:group) of all bijections $X\to X$, the [permutations](c:permutation) of $X$, with composition as the product. For $X=\{1,\dots,n\}$ it is written $S_n$, and it has $n!$ elements.
examples: $S_3$ has $6$ elements: the identity, three transpositions and two $3$-cycles.
$S_2$ has two elements and is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is not a symmetric group $S_n$, because $|S_n|=n!$ is never $3$.

steps: A [permutation group](c:permutation-group) on $X$ is a subgroup of the group of bijections of $X$.
Take the subgroup $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ itself, which contains every bijection.
So $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ is a permutation group on $X$, and it is the largest one.
links.why: It shows that every permutation group is a subgroup of a symmetric group.

steps: Take the category of sets, whose morphisms are functions.
An automorphism of $X$ in this category is an invertible function, that is, a bijection $X\to X$.
Composition makes these bijections into the group $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$.
So $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ is the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of $X$ in the category of sets.
links.why: It shows that the symmetric group is the automorphism group of a bare set.

reminder: A square matrix $A$ is symmetric when it equals its [transpose](c:transpose-matrix), $A^T=A$.
definition: A square [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ is symmetric when $A^T=A$, where $A^T$ is the [transpose matrix](c:transpose-matrix); that is, $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$. Its entries are mirror images across the main diagonal.
examples: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric.
Every [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) is symmetric.
For every matrix $B$, the products $B^TB$ and $BB^T$ are symmetric.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric, because $a_{12}=2\ne0=a_{21}$.

steps: Take a diagonal matrix $D$, so $d_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$.
Then $d_{ij}=d_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, because the off-diagonal entries are $0$ on both sides.
So $D^T=D$, and $D$ is symmetric.
A symmetric matrix may have nonzero off-diagonal entries, as long as they mirror each other.
links.why: It shows that symmetric matrices include the diagonal ones and allow mirrored entries off the diagonal.

steps: Take a real symmetric matrix $A$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product.
For all vectors $x,y$ we have $\langle Ax,y\rangle=y^TAx=(A^Ty)^Tx=\langle x,A^Ty\rangle$.
Since $A^T=A$, this equals $\langle x,Ay\rangle$.
So $A$ is self-adjoint: $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
links.why: It shows that real symmetric matrices are the self-adjoint operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the spectral theorem applies.

reminder: A symmetric [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) has a swap $A\otimes B\cong B\otimes A$ whose double swap is the identity.
definition: A symmetric monoidal category is a [braided monoidal category](c:braided-monoidal-category) $(\mathcal C,\otimes,I,\sigma)$ whose braiding $\sigma_{A,B}:A\otimes B\to B\otimes A$ satisfies $\sigma_{B,A}\circ\sigma_{A,B}=\mathrm{id}_{A\otimes B}$. The braiding is a [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism) that is compatible with the associator and the unit of the [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category), by the hexagon equations.
examples: Sets with the cartesian product and the swap $(a,b)\mapsto(b,a)$ form a symmetric monoidal category.
Vector spaces over a field $k$ with $\otimes_k$ and the swap $v\otimes w\mapsto w\otimes v$ form a symmetric monoidal category.
Non-example: representations of a quantum group at generic $q$ form a braided monoidal category whose braiding has $\sigma_{B,A}\sigma_{A,B}\ne\mathrm{id}$, so it is braided but not symmetric.

steps: Take a symmetric monoidal category with symmetry $\sigma$.
The hexagon equations hold, because they are part of its definition as a braided monoidal category.
So $\sigma$ is a braiding, and the category is a [braided monoidal category](c:braided-monoidal-category).
The symmetric case adds that $\sigma_{B,A}\sigma_{A,B}=\mathrm{id}$ for all objects $A,B$.
links.why: It shows that a symmetry is a braiding that squares to the identity.

steps: Take a category with finite products and its cartesian monoidal structure $A\times B$.
The swap $A\times B\to B\times A$ that exchanges the two projections is natural in $A$ and $B$.
It is its own inverse and satisfies the hexagon equations.
So every [cartesian monoidal category](c:cartesian-monoidal-category) is symmetric monoidal.
links.why: It shows that cartesian products always come with a symmetry, so the symmetric theory covers them.

reminder: A family of [probability measures](c:probability-measure) is tight when almost all of the mass of every member lies in one [compact](c:compact-space) set.
definition: A family $\{\mu_i\}_{i\in I}$ of [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is tight when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a [compact](c:compact-space) set $K\subseteq X$ with $\mu_i(K)\ge1-\varepsilon$ for all $i\in I$. On a Polish space, every single probability measure is tight.
examples: Every finite family of probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ is tight.
The Gaussian measures $N(m,1)$ with $|m|\le5$ form a tight family on $\mathbb{R}$: take $K=[-R,R]$ with $R$ large.
Non-example: the point masses $\delta_n$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are not tight, because every compact set $K$ has $\delta_n(K)=0$ for large $n$.

reminder: Time reversal maps a state or a trajectory to the one that runs backward in time.
definition: In classical mechanics on a [phase space](c:phase-space) with coordinates $(q,p)$, time reversal is the map $T(q,p)=(q,-p)$, which sends a trajectory $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ to $t\mapsto(q(-t),-p(-t))$. In quantum mechanics on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), it is an [antiunitary operator](c:antiunitary-operator) $\Theta$ that reverses momentum and spin, and a Hamiltonian $H$ is time-reversal symmetric when $\Theta H\Theta^{-1}=H$.
examples: A free particle with $q(t)=vt$ and $p=mv$ becomes the trajectory $q(t)=-vt$, $p=-mv$, which is also a free motion.
For a spin-$1/2$ particle, $\Theta=i\sigma_yK$ with $K$ complex conjugation, and $\Theta^2=-1$.
Non-example: the time evolution $\psi\mapsto e^{-iHt}\psi$ is not time reversal, because it runs forward in time and is linear, while $\Theta$ is antilinear.

reminder: A topological space is a set with a topology: a family of open sets closed under unions and finite intersections.
definition: A topological space is a [set](c:set) $X$ with a family $\tau$ of subsets of $X$, that is, a subset of the [power set](c:power-set) $\mathcal P(X)$, such that $\varnothing\in\tau$, $X\in\tau$, the [union](c:union) of any family of members of $\tau$ is in $\tau$, and the [intersection](c:intersection) of finitely many members of $\tau$ is in $\tau$. The members of $\tau$ are called the open sets.
examples: Every [metric space](c:metric-space) is a topological space: the open sets are the unions of open balls, so $\mathbb{R}^n$ has its usual topology.
Any set $X$ with $\tau=\mathcal P(X)$ (the discrete topology) or with $\tau=\{\varnothing,X\}$ (the indiscrete topology) is a topological space.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}$, the family of open intervals together with $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$ is not a topology, because the union $(0,1)\cup(2,3)$ is missing.

steps: Take a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ and its open balls $B(x,r)$.
Call a set $U$ open when it is a union of open balls.
The empty set and $X$ are open, and any union of open sets is open.
A finite intersection of open sets is open, by the triangle inequality, so the open sets form a topology.
links.why: It shows that every metric space is a topological space, so topological results apply to metric spaces.

steps: Take a [total order](c:total-order) on $X$ and the open rays $\{y:y<a\}$ and $\{y:y>a\}$.
Let $\tau$ be the family of all unions of finite intersections of these rays.
Then $\tau$ contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, and it is closed under unions and finite intersections.
So $(X,\tau)$ is a topological space, the order topology.
links.why: It shows that every totally ordered set has a natural topology, so ordered sets are topological spaces.

reminder: A total order is a [partial order](c:partial-order) in which any two elements are comparable.
definition: A total order on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a binary relation $\le$ that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, so it is a [partial order](c:partial-order), and that is also total: for all $x,y\in X$, $x\le y$ or $y\le x$.
examples: The real numbers with the usual order $\le$ form a total order.
Words in a dictionary form a total order, the lexicographic order.
Non-example: the subsets of $\{1,2\}$ ordered by inclusion form a partial order but not a total order, because $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are not comparable.

steps: Take a total order $\le$ on $X$.
By definition it is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, so it is a [partial order](c:partial-order).
The total case adds that every two elements are comparable.
links.why: It shows that a total order is a partial order with no incomparable pairs.

steps: Take a [well order](c:well-order) $\le$ on $X$, so every nonempty subset has a least element.
For any $x,y$, the subset $\{x,y\}$ has a least element, so $x\le y$ or $y\le x$.
So $\le$ is total, and a well order is a total order with the extra least-element property.
links.why: It shows that a well order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element.

reminder: A [metric space](c:metric-space) is totally bounded when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, finitely many [balls](c:ball) of radius $\varepsilon$ cover it.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is totally bounded when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are finitely many points $x_1,\dots,x_m$ such that the [balls](c:ball) $B(x_i,\varepsilon)$ form a [finite cover](c:finite-cover) of $X$. Equivalently, every sequence in $X$ has a Cauchy subsequence.
examples: Every bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is totally bounded.
$[0,1]$ is totally bounded: for every $\varepsilon>0$, finitely many intervals of length $\varepsilon$ cover it.
Non-example: an infinite set with the metric $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$ is bounded but not totally bounded, because the balls of radius $1/2$ are single points.

steps: Take a totally bounded metric space $X$ and cover it by finitely many balls $B(x_i,1)$.
Every point lies within distance $1$ of some $x_i$, and the finitely many centres lie within a fixed distance $D$ of each other.
So any two points are within distance $D+2$, and $X$ is [bounded](c:bounded-space).
The converse fails: an infinite discrete space is bounded but not totally bounded.
links.why: It shows that total boundedness is boundedness at every scale $\varepsilon$, not only at one scale.

steps: Take a compact metric space $X$ and a number $\varepsilon>0$.
The open balls $B(x,\varepsilon)$ for $x\in X$ cover $X$.
By compactness, finitely many of them cover $X$, so $X$ is totally bounded.
A metric space is compact exactly when it is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) that is totally bounded.
links.why: It shows that compactness gives total boundedness, and that completeness is the missing part.

reminder: A tree is a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) that has no [cycles](c:cycle).
definition: A tree is a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) that contains no [cycle](c:cycle). Equivalently, any two vertices are joined by exactly one [path](c:path), and a tree with $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges.
examples: A path with $n$ vertices is a tree.
A star, with one centre joined to $n$ leaves, is a tree.
Non-example: a cycle graph $C_n$ with $n\ge3$ is connected but contains a cycle, and two disjoint edges form an acyclic graph that is not connected, so neither is a tree.

steps: Take a tree $T$.
By definition $T$ has no cycle, so it is an [acyclic graph](c:acyclic-graph).
The tree case adds that $T$ is connected, while an acyclic graph may have several components.
links.why: It shows that a tree is a connected acyclic graph, and that an acyclic graph is a union of trees.

steps: Take a tree $T$.
By definition $T$ is a [connected graph](c:connected-graph).
The tree case adds that $T$ has no cycle, so removing any edge disconnects it.
links.why: It shows that a tree is a connected graph with no redundant edge.

steps: Take a [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree), a tree with one vertex chosen as the root.
Forget the root and keep only the vertices and the edges.
What remains is a connected graph with no cycle, that is, a tree.
Conversely, choosing any vertex of a tree as the root gives a rooted tree.
links.why: It shows that a rooted tree is a tree with one chosen vertex, so tree results apply to rooted trees.

reminder: A triangulation of a space $Y$ is a [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) whose geometric realization is homeomorphic to $Y$.
definition: A triangulation of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $Y$ is a [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) $K$ together with a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $h:|K|\to Y$, where $|K|$ is the [geometric realization](c:geometric-realization) of $K$. More generally, $K$ may be a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) with its geometric realization $|K|$.
examples: The boundary of a tetrahedron, with four triangles, six edges and four vertices, is a triangulation of the sphere $S^2$.
Every smooth manifold has a triangulation.
Non-example: a filled triangle is not a triangulation of the circle $S^1$, because its realization is a disk; the three edges alone, without the inside, are a triangulation.

steps: Take a triangulation of a polygon $P$ by non-crossing diagonals.
Its triangles, edges and vertices form a [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) $K$ in the plane.
The union of the triangles is $P$, so the realization $|K|$ is homeomorphic to $P$.
So this is a triangulation of the topological space $P$.
links.why: It shows that triangulating a polygon is the planar special case of triangulating a space.

reminder: An unbiased estimator has an [expected value](c:expected-value) equal to the parameter it estimates, whatever the parameter is.
definition: Let $X$ be data from a distribution with an unknown parameter $\theta$. An estimator $T(X)$ of $\theta$, a [statistic](c:statistic) used as a guess for $\theta$, is unbiased when the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the [random variable](c:random-variable) $T(X)$ satisfies $E_\theta[T(X)]=\theta$ for every possible value of $\theta$. Then the bias $E_\theta[T(X)]-\theta$ is zero.
examples: The sample mean $\bar X$ is an unbiased estimator of the mean $\mu$, because $E[\bar X]=\mu$.
The sample variance with divisor $n-1$ is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$ for independent samples.
Non-example: the sample variance with divisor $n$ has expected value $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$, so it is biased.

steps: Take an unbiased estimator $T$ of a parameter $\theta$.
Then $T(X)$ is a function of the data alone, and it does not use the unknown $\theta$, so it is a [statistic](c:statistic).
The unbiased case adds the condition $E_\theta[T(X)]=\theta$ for every $\theta$.
links.why: It shows that unbiasedness is a condition on a statistic that is used as an estimator.

reminder: A unimodular lattice is an integral [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) that equals its [dual lattice](c:dual-lattice).
definition: A [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) $L\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ of rank $n$ is unimodular when $\langle x,y\rangle\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $x,y\in L$ and $L$ equals its [dual lattice](c:dual-lattice) $L^*=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,y\rangle\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for all }y\in L\}$, using the [inner product](c:inner-product-space). Equivalently, the Gram matrix of a basis has integer entries and [determinant](c:determinant) $1$; for an integral lattice with a nondegenerate symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) the determinant may also be $-1$.
examples: $\mathbb{Z}^n$ with the standard dot product is unimodular.
The [E8 lattice](c:e8-lattice) is an even unimodular lattice in $\mathbb{R}^8$.
Non-example: the hexagonal lattice with Gram matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $3$, so it is not unimodular.

steps: Take a unimodular lattice $L\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.
It is a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^n$ of rank $n$, so it is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup).
The unimodular case adds that $\langle x,y\rangle\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $x,y\in L$ and that $L^*=L$.
links.why: It shows that unimodularity is an arithmetic condition on a lattice, tied to its inner product.

steps: Take the $E_8$ lattice with its Gram matrix, the Cartan matrix of $E_8$.
This is an integer matrix with even diagonal entries.
Its determinant is $1$, so the lattice is integral and equals its dual.
So $E_8$ is a unimodular lattice, and it is even.
links.why: It shows that the E8 lattice is the standard even unimodular lattice of rank $8$.
